original_question: Is every non-trivial (a, b)-geproci set forced to contain three collinear points, or can one construct a counterexample?
target_in_paper: Section 3, Problem 3.7: "Prove or disprove (by giving a counterexample) that every non-trivial (a, b)-geproci set has a subset of 3 collinear points."
correct_elements: Your draft is very close to the paper's actual target. It correctly identifies the right class of objects ((a, b)-geproci sets), the right qualifier (non-trivial), the exact geometric property under discussion (existence of a collinear triple), and the correct proof/disproof format (either prove necessity or produce a counterexample).
missing_details: The ambient setting is a finite set Z of points in P^3, not an abstract incidence configuration and not a geproci set in arbitrary P^n.

(a, b)-geproci must be defined: for a general projection from a point P to a plane H isomorphic to P^2, the image of Z is the transverse complete intersection of plane curves C_{a,P} and C_{b,P} of degrees a and b, with a <= b.
From that definition one also gets the implicit cardinality condition |Z| = ab.
"Non-trivial" has a paper-specific meaning: it excludes the easy, well-understood cases of degenerate geproci sets and (a, b)-grids.

To make the exclusion stand-alone, an (a, b)-grid should be defined as the set of ab pairwise intersection points of a skew lines and b skew lines in P^3, each line from one family meeting each line from the other family exactly once.
"Has three collinear points" should be stated as: Z contains a 3-point subset lying on a line in P^3.
The paper does not impose an extra field or characteristic restriction in Problem 3.7, so a faithful rewrite should not add one.
Problem 3.8 is only a more general neighboring problem about linearly general geproci sets; it should not replace Problem 3.7.
refined_question: Let Z be a finite subset of P^3 such that for a general point P, the projection of Z from P to a plane H isomorphic to P^2 is the transverse complete intersection C_{a,P} intersect C_{b,P} of plane curves of degrees a <= b; equivalently, Z is an (a, b)-geproci set, so |Z| = ab. Assume Z is non-trivial in the sense of the paper, namely that Z is neither one of the degenerate geproci examples already lying in a hyperplane as a complete intersection there nor an (a, b)-grid (the ab intersection points of a skew lines with b skew lines in P^3, each line from one family meeting each line from the other exactly once). Must every such non-trivial (a, b)-geproci set contain a 3-point collinear subset, or does there exist a counterexample with no three collinear points?
justification: The draft is aiming at Problem 3.7 almost verbatim. The surrounding paragraph in Section 3 supplies the needed definitions of geproci, (a, b)-geproci, grids, halfgrids/non-halfgrids, and the paper's use of "trivial." It is not Problem 3.6, which asks for non-trivial (a, b)-geproci sets where the projected curves are not unexpected, and it should not be broadened to Problem 3.8, which asks more generally for a linearly general geproci set.
